title: Colombia's Election Eve: A Forking Path Between Total Peace Continuation and Security Crackdown
detail: Four days before Colombia's pivotal May 31 presidential election, International Crisis Group characterized the vote as a defining moment for the future of the Total Peace policy and the country's 2016 FARC peace accords. Front-runner Iván Cepeda (Historic Pact, left, ~44% in polls) pledged to continue and deepen peace negotiations with all armed groups. Right-wing challengers Paloma Valencia (Centro Democrático) and Abelardo de la Espriella have vowed to suspend talks with groups that continue violence, resume aerial fumigation, and pursue a hard-line security approach akin to Uribe's 2002–2010 Democratic Security policy. The campaign ended as the bloodiest in decades: 61 political leaders killed, 139 municipalities at extreme electoral risk, a journalist murdered, journalist attacks up 175%, and the U.S. warning it may not recognize results. No candidate was projected to reach the 50% threshold for a first-round win; a June runoff is considered near-certain. Whichever candidate wins will inherit Petro's stalled peace process, record armed-group growth, and Colombia's worst displacement figures in a decade.

media.caption: Colombia's May 31 election marks a forking path between peace talks and a security crackdown
